context.concept_name: Run supplied unit and integration tests as blocking pipeline gates after external testing preparation

coverage.learning_objective: Run supplied tests as blocking pipeline gates

required_facts.statement: A nonzero command exit status reports failure to a pipeline step, while zero reports success.
Run the supplied unit and integration test commands in workflow steps with run: TEST_COMMAND; set the promotion job’s needs: [UNIT_JOB, INTEGRATION_JOB] to require both test jobs.
Do not set continue-on-error on the blocking test steps; demonstrate a failing supplied test prevents the dependent promotion.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A promotion job must require both supplied unit and integration tests. Make failure visible to the workflow and preserve the dependency on both jobs rather than allowing promotion to ignore a failing test.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A nonzero command exit status reports failure to a pipeline step, while zero reports success.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Run the supplied unit and integration test commands in workflow steps with run: TEST_COMMAND; set the promotion job’s needs: [UNIT_JOB, INTEGRATION_JOB] to require both test jobs.

Do not set continue-on-error on the blocking test steps; demonstrate a failing supplied test prevents the dependent promotion.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Run the supplied TEST_COMMAND values in test steps and set the promotion job's needs to the supplied unit and integration job names. Do not set continue-on-error on blocking test steps. Use the seeded failing test and inspect its nonzero exit result and the dependent promotion outcome. Record that the test failure prevents promotion; an independently successful other test is not enough to satisfy both gates.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A command that failed must not be converted into a tolerated blocking-test result with continue-on-error. The promotion dependency requires both test jobs, and the supplied failure case demonstrates that progression is blocked.

video_need.reason: A seeded test failure and blocked dependent promotion benefit from a short workflow execution demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Wire the supplied unit and integration test commands into separate jobs in one prepared GitHub Actions workflow. Require both jobs for promotion, leave continue-on-error unset on blocking test steps, and run the supplied seeded failure case.
practice_anchor.success: The failing supplied test reports a nonzero exit status, its job fails, and the dependent promotion job is skipped even when the other test job succeeds.

live_code.required_skill: Configure supplied test commands as blocking workflow steps and make promotion depend on both test jobs.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide a runnable sandbox workflow with prepared runner and application setup, supplied UNIT_JOB and INTEGRATION_JOB names, supplied TEST_COMMAND values, and a harmless promotion job. Include a prepared seeded failing test case; learners modify only the test steps and promotion dependencies.
live_code.observable_success: Both supplied test commands appear in their respective jobs, promotion declares both jobs in needs, and neither blocking test step sets continue-on-error. Execution shows a nonzero test result, a failed test job, a successful other test job, and skipped promotion.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the workflow dependency and execution outcomes visible: both test jobs feed promotion, one supplied test job fails, the other succeeds, and promotion is skipped. Show the failing command's nonzero exit status.

teaching_notes: Use supplied tests; do not teach application test authoring or unfamiliar shell exit-handling syntax.

context.concept_name: Submit small reviewable infrastructure changes after registry Git and code-review prerequisites

coverage.learning_objective: Submit a small reviewable infrastructure change

required_facts.statement: Small coherent changes reduce review complexity and make delivery feedback easier to act on.

In the supplied repository workflow, stage the focused files with git add FILES, commit with git commit -m "MESSAGE", push the review branch with git push, and open its supplied pull-request interface to request review.
Submit a focused infrastructure pull request with its intent, coherent diff and saved plan evidence showing the affected EC2 resource.
After the supplied approval, execute the supplied CI apply using the approved saved plan and attach the execution and resource-verification evidence to the change record.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A small infrastructure change should be understandable at review and traceable through approved execution. Keep intent, focused diff, saved plan and resource verification in one change record.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Small coherent changes reduce review complexity and make delivery feedback easier to act on.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
In the supplied repository workflow, stage the focused files with git add FILES, commit with git commit -m "MESSAGE", push the review branch with git push, and open its supplied pull-request interface to request review.

Submit a focused infrastructure pull request with its intent, coherent diff and saved plan evidence showing the affected EC2 resource.

After the supplied approval, execute the supplied CI apply using the approved saved plan and attach the execution and resource-verification evidence to the change record.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Stage only the focused supplied files, commit with a descriptive supplied message and push the review branch through the established Git workflow. Open its supplied pull-request interface to request review. Include the change's intent, coherent diff and saved plan evidence for the affected EC2 resource. After supplied approval, run the supplied CI apply with that approved saved plan and attach execution plus resource-verification evidence. The example carries one focused change from review to verified outcome instead of mixing unrelated modifications into the submission.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Review approval alone is not the execution record. Retain the approved saved plan, supplied CI apply outcome and live-resource verification. A small coherent diff improves reviewability but still needs those execution checks.

video_need.reason: A short focused diff/plan/approval/execution record walkthrough helps show traceability, while the bounded review workflow is explicit in text.

practice_anchor.objective: Submit one focused Terraform EC2 pull request through the supplied repository and review interface. Stage the focused files, commit and push the review branch, and include intent, a coherent diff and saved-plan evidence. After the supplied reviewer approves it, run the supplied CI apply workflow using the approved saved plan and attach execution and EC2 resource-verification evidence. Independent impact authorization is not reassessed.
practice_anchor.success: The change record contains one coherent EC2 change, a traceable commit, clear intent, saved-plan evidence identifying the affected EC2 resource, supplied reviewer approval, a successful CI execution using that approved saved plan, and verification of the resulting single EC2 instance.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the supplied pull-request record visible with its focused diff, intent, commit reference, saved-plan evidence for the EC2 resource, reviewer approval, CI execution result and resulting instance verification.

teaching_notes: Require external Git/CI preparation; use supplied review interface and approved apply workflow.

context.concept_name: Verify availability across Availability Zones under a controlled failure

required_facts.statement: Resilience testing deliberately introduces failures to verify the workload can meet its availability requirements.
Limit the approved failure to the supplied AZ components, define abort criteria, and monitor client-visible service behavior during the experiment.
Check that the remaining independent capacity and request path maintain the required service behavior rather than inferring availability from surviving instance count alone.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A workload has capacity in more than one Availability Zone, but the controlled test must show required client-visible behavior during an approved AZ-component loss. Surviving resources alone do not establish availability.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Resilience testing deliberately introduces failures to verify the workload can meet its availability requirements.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Limit the approved failure to the supplied AZ components, define abort criteria, and monitor client-visible service behavior during the experiment.

Check that the remaining independent capacity and request path maintain the required service behavior rather than inferring availability from surviving instance count alone.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Define the approved AZ-scoped failure and abort criteria before the experiment. During the supplied failure, monitor the client-visible service behavior. Compare the remaining independent capacity and request path with the service requirement. Suppose some instances survive but clients cannot complete the required request: record that the availability criterion was not demonstrated, rather than calling the test passed from the survivor count. Keep the failure scope, observed client behavior and remaining-path evidence together. This is deliberate resilience verification within supplied limits, not an exercise to disable an entire Region or infer availability from the existence of multiple locations.

For a passing result, retain the client check that demonstrates required behavior along with the surviving path and capacity observations. If remaining resources exist but the request path fails, the availability criterion has not been met. These two contrasting cases show why the experiment monitors the service from the client perspective instead of treating resource survival as an automatic availability proof.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A surviving instance count is not a client-visible availability result. Verify that remaining independent capacity and the request path maintain the required behavior, and keep the experiment within the approved AZ components and abort limits.

video_need.reason: An AZ-scoped loss and surviving client request path benefit from a failure-domain diagram tied to observed service behavior.

practice_anchor.objective: Run the supplied approved AZ-component failure procedure in a two-AZ topology. Confirm the target components and define abort criteria before starting, monitor required client-visible behavior during the failure, and check the remaining independent capacity and request path.
practice_anchor.success: Only the approved components in one AZ are affected, the defined abort criteria are enforced, and the result is judged against the supplied service requirement using client-request outcomes and remaining-path evidence rather than surviving instance count alone.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the supplied two-AZ topology with the approved failed components marked, the remaining independent capacity and client request path identified, and observed client-request outcomes compared with the required service behavior.

teaching_notes: Use approved failure procedure; do not introduce regional failover or unsafe production faults.

required_facts.statement: Resource deletion must respect dependencies; CloudFormation uses resource relationships when deleting a stack.
Identify only the supplied exercise resources by stack membership or approved tags, remove dependent resources before their prerequisites and verify deletion results.
An S3 bucket must be empty before deletion; remove the exercise bucket’s objects, all object versions and delete markers before deleting that bucket.
Retained resources and failed deletions need explicit inspection and approved follow-up; a completed deletion operation is not billing verification.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Exercise teardown should remove only approved resources in dependency order. The operator also needs to inspect what was retained or failed to delete, without claiming deletion completion is billing verification.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Resource deletion must respect dependencies; CloudFormation uses resource relationships when deleting a stack.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Identify only the supplied exercise resources by stack membership or approved tags, remove dependent resources before their prerequisites and verify deletion results.

An S3 bucket must be empty before deletion; remove the exercise bucket’s objects, all object versions and delete markers before deleting that bucket.

Retained resources and failed deletions need explicit inspection and approved follow-up; a completed deletion operation is not billing verification.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Identify exercise resources by approved stack membership or tags. Remove dependents before their prerequisites and verify deletion results. For the supplied S3 bucket, empty objects, all object versions and delete markers before deleting the bucket; a current listing alone is not the stated version cleanup. Inspect any retained resources and failed deletions for approved follow-up. CloudFormation uses resource relationships during stack deletion, but that does not remove the need to inspect retained or failed resources. Keep the scope and per-resource deletion evidence in the cleanup record. A completed deletion operation is not a proof of zero charge: this task verifies resource removal, while the later billing check verifies residual charges.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Deleting a versioned bucket requires emptying versions and delete markers as well as objects. Also, a completed deletion operation is not billing verification. Inspect retained resources and deletion failures rather than assuming every exercise resource disappeared.

video_need.reason: Dependent-first removal, versioned-bucket contents and retained/failed resources benefit from a scoped teardown sequence diagram.

practice_anchor.objective: Delete one supplied tagged sandbox exercise using approved tags or stack membership to establish scope. Remove dependents before prerequisites, empty the exercise S3 bucket of objects, all object versions and delete markers before deleting it, and inspect deletion results.
practice_anchor.success: Only approved exercise resources are targeted, and unrelated resources remain unchanged. Removal respects dependencies, including complete bucket-content cleanup before bucket deletion. Each deletion result is inspected; retained resources and failures are identified for approved follow-up rather than treated as removed. Completion is reported as a resource-removal result, not billing verification.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the approved exercise boundary and dependent-first removal sequence visible. Show objects, all object versions and delete markers being removed before the S3 bucket, CloudFormation using resource relationships during stack deletion, and deletion results branching into confirmed removal or retained/failed resources requiring inspection and approved follow-up. Keep billing verification outside this teardown flow.

teaching_notes: Use approved scope and dependency order; leave residual-charge verification to its later concept.

required_facts.statement: Recovery execution needs a valid, unexpired session with the permissions required for backup access and resource creation.
Establish the approved recovery session, inspect its identity and expiry, and test the supplied backup-read and recovery-resource operations before rehearsal.
A valid credential lifetime does not prove sufficient authorization; verify both access outcomes and lifetime.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Recovery rehearsal needs a valid session that can perform the required work. Check lifetime and authorization independently before using it for restoration.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Recovery execution needs a valid, unexpired session with the permissions required for backup access and resource creation.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Establish the approved recovery session, inspect its identity and expiry, and test the supplied backup-read and recovery-resource operations before rehearsal.

A valid credential lifetime does not prove sufficient authorization; verify both access outcomes and lifetime.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Establish the approved recovery session and inspect its identity and expiry. Test the supplied backup-read and recovery-resource operations. Record both outcomes alongside the credential lifetime. If the credentials are unexpired but the backup-read test is denied, they are not ready for the required recovery. Conversely, permission evidence does not remove the need for a valid session during execution.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Unexpired credentials do not prove sufficient authorization. Recovery readiness needs both valid lifetime and successful required access tests for backup reading and resource creation.

video_need.reason: A short identity/expiry/access check helps distinguish session validity from authorization, while text states both readiness requirements.

practice_anchor.objective: Test one approved recovery session before rehearsal using the supplied identity, expiry, backup-read, and recovery-resource checks without exposing credentials.
practice_anchor.success: The approved session is established, its identity and expiry are inspected, and both supplied operation outcomes are recorded alongside its lifetime. Readiness requires the expected identity, a valid unexpired session, and successful backup-read and recovery-resource operations; an unexpired session with a denied operation is identified as not ready.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the approved recovery session's identity and expiry alongside the supplied backup-read and recovery-resource test outcomes, making lifetime and authorization separately visible without displaying credentials.

teaching_notes: Use approved session provider and safe supplied tests; do not expose credentials.

required_facts.statement: Recovery testing should use a controlled environment that limits the experiment’s effects.
Prepare the supplied isolated account and network target and check restoration destinations and client test traffic do not point to production.
Record the approved scope and stop conditions before provisioning recovery resources or directing test traffic.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A recovery rehearsal must stay inside the approved environment. Confirm restoration destinations and test traffic before provisioning resources, not only after clients begin using them.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Recovery testing should use a controlled environment that limits the experiment’s effects.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Prepare the supplied isolated account and network target and check restoration destinations and client test traffic do not point to production.

Record the approved scope and stop conditions before provisioning recovery resources or directing test traffic.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Prepare the supplied isolated account and network target. Inspect restoration destinations and client test traffic settings to confirm they do not point to production. Record approved scope and stop conditions before provisioning or redirecting traffic. Keep those settings beside the rehearsal record so isolation is evidence of the actual targets, not just a label on the exercise.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Calling an account a sandbox is not the complete isolation check. Restoration destinations and client traffic must also stay out of production, and approved scope/stop conditions must be recorded before the experiment acts.

video_need.reason: A short rehearsal-target and client-traffic diagram helps verify isolation without introducing a new environment design.

practice_anchor.objective: Prepare one recovery target using the supplied isolated account and network boundaries. Inspect restoration destinations and client test traffic settings, and record the approved scope and stop conditions before provisioning resources or directing test traffic.
practice_anchor.success: The prepared target uses the supplied isolated account and network. Restoration destinations and client test traffic settings do not point to production, and the approved scope and stop conditions are recorded before any provisioning or test traffic begins.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the supplied isolated account and network boundaries visible, with restoration destinations and client test traffic paths confined to the recovery target and production clearly outside those paths.

teaching_notes: Use supplied isolated target; do not create production cutover or new network-isolation design.

coverage.learning_objective: Gate automated response with approvals and stop controls

required_facts.statement: An aws:approve Automation step pauses execution pending approval or rejection by the designated approvers.
Put the approval step before the protected operation and use the supplied branching or failure path to prevent that operation on rejection or stop.
Stop an Automation execution with the approved stop operation when a stop condition occurs and inspect execution state before allowing further actions.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A protected Automation operation requires approval and an enforceable stop path. Position that decision before the operation and inspect the actual execution state when stopping.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An aws:approve Automation step pauses execution pending approval or rejection by the designated approvers.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Put the approval step before the protected operation and use the supplied branching or failure path to prevent that operation on rejection or stop.

Stop an Automation execution with the approved stop operation when a stop condition occurs and inspect execution state before allowing further actions.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Place the supplied aws:approve step before the protected action. Use the established branching or failure path so rejection or stop prevents that operation. In the supplied stop-condition test, use the approved stop operation and inspect execution state before allowing further actions. The approval step pauses for designated approvers; it is not authorization to run the protected action before they decide.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An approval request is not an approval outcome. Rejection or stop must prevent the protected operation, and a stop request still requires inspecting execution state before further action is allowed.

video_need.reason: Approval pause, rejection/stop and protected-action state benefit from a short controlled Automation execution demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Add the supplied aws:approve gate before the protected operation in a bounded remediation workflow. Connect the supplied rejection or failure path, then use the approved stop operation when the supplied stop condition occurs.
practice_anchor.success: The workflow pauses for designated approvers before the protected operation. Pending approval, rejection, and stop do not permit that operation. After requesting a stop, execution state is inspected before any further action is allowed.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the approval step's position before the protected operation visible, together with pending, rejected, and stopped execution states and the protected operation remaining unexecuted in each case.

teaching_notes: Use supplied branching and stop operation; do not invent Automation document syntax.

required_facts.statement: Automation execution details include an execution identifier, step statuses, inputs, outputs and failure information.
Record execution ID, acting role, target identities, start/end times and per-step outcomes for the supplied response.
Use CloudTrail request identity and operation evidence to attribute the underlying AWS actions; success and failure outcomes both belong in the response record.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An operational response needs an audit record for successful and failed steps. Connect the Automation execution context with CloudTrail evidence of the underlying AWS actions.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Automation execution details include an execution identifier, step statuses, inputs, outputs and failure information.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Record execution ID, acting role, target identities, start/end times and per-step outcomes for the supplied response.

Use CloudTrail request identity and operation evidence to attribute the underlying AWS actions; success and failure outcomes both belong in the response record.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Record the execution ID, acting role, targets, start/end times and per-step outcomes from the supplied response. Inspect inputs, outputs and failure information as part of that record. Use CloudTrail request identity and operation evidence to attribute the AWS actions. If a step failed, retain its evidence rather than omitting it from a success-focused summary. This makes the record describe what the response actually attempted and achieved.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Audit evidence is not only a list of successful steps. Inputs, outputs, failure information and attributed underlying operations all matter. Keep both success and failure outcomes with the execution identity and targets.

video_need.reason: A short execution-to-CloudTrail evidence walkthrough helps locate step outcomes and attributed operations; text covers the required record.

practice_anchor.objective: Capture the execution ID, acting role, target identities, start/end times and per-step outcomes for one supplied response run. Include inputs, outputs and failure information, and select CloudTrail request identity and operation evidence that attributes the underlying AWS actions.
practice_anchor.success: The completed response record accurately captures the supplied execution identifiers, authority, targets, times and step details, links underlying actions to CloudTrail evidence, and retains both successful and failed outcomes without inferring actions from the intended plan.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make one supplied response run's execution ID, acting role, targets, start/end times, step statuses, inputs, outputs and failure information visible alongside the corresponding CloudTrail request identity and operation evidence.

teaching_notes: Use supplied execution/CloudTrail records; do not infer actions from the operator’s intended plan.

required_facts.statement: CloudTrail log-file integrity validation uses signed digest files and hashes to detect modification or deletion of delivered log files.

Run aws cloudtrail validate-logs --trail-arn ARN --start-time TIME --end-time TIME --region REGION against the supplied log/digest interval and inspect validation failures; for an organization trail also provide the required --account-id.
Digest validation supplies tamper evidence but does not itself prevent unauthorized access or deletion.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Audit logs need tamper evidence as well as storage controls. CloudTrail digest validation checks the delivered log interval; it does not itself prevent someone from accessing or deleting the files.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: CloudTrail log-file integrity validation uses signed digest files and hashes to detect modification or deletion of delivered log files.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Run aws cloudtrail validate-logs --trail-arn ARN --start-time TIME --end-time TIME --region REGION against the supplied log/digest interval and inspect validation failures; for an organization trail also provide the required --account-id.

Digest validation supplies tamper evidence but does not itself prevent unauthorized access or deletion.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Substitute the supplied trail ARN, start/end times and Region into aws cloudtrail validate-logs. For an organization trail, include the required --account-id for the supplied account. Inspect validation failures for that log/digest interval. The validation uses signed digest files and hashes to detect modification or deletion of delivered logs. Keep the interval and validation result in the evidence record rather than declaring all logs intact from an unrelated successful interval. A passing validation result is tamper-evidence verification for the checked material, not an authorization control or prevention of future deletion.

Keep validation scope explicit in the result: trail identity, account when required, selected interval and Region. A failure is evidence to preserve and investigate under the supplied procedure, not a reason to omit the affected files from the record. Authorization and retention still need their own controls because knowing that material was changed or deleted is not the same as preventing that action.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Digest validation detects tampering; it does not prevent unauthorized access or deletion. Run it on the supplied log/digest interval and preserve failure evidence, keeping that role distinct from access and retention controls.

video_need.reason: Digest validation over a selected interval and its failure evidence benefit from observing the supplied tamper-check operation.

practice_anchor.objective: Validate one supplied CloudTrail log/digest set using aws cloudtrail validate-logs with the supplied trail ARN, start time, end time and Region, including --account-id when required for an organization trail. Inspect the result and identify the seeded integrity failure.
practice_anchor.success: The validation targets the supplied trail, interval, Region and account when required. The learner identifies the seeded failure from the supplied validation results, preserves its evidence with the validation scope, and does not treat validation as prevention of unauthorized access or deletion.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the validation command's trail, interval, Region and required account scope visible alongside the supplied validation results, with the seeded integrity failure identifiable.

teaching_notes: Include organization-trail account-id where required; do not invent validation output or claim preventive protection.

required_facts.statement: S3 Object Lock applies retention to object versions using governance or compliance mode and a retain-until date.
Apply the supplied default retention duration and mode on the prepared Object Lock bucket and inspect individual audit-object version retention.
Compliance mode prevents deletion or shortening of retention during the retention period even by root; governance mode permits bypass only with the necessary bypass authorization and request.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Audit retention applies to individual object versions, and the selected Object Lock mode changes what bypass is possible. Verify version retention rather than inspecting only the bucket default.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: S3 Object Lock applies retention to object versions using governance or compliance mode and a retain-until date.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Apply the supplied default retention duration and mode on the prepared Object Lock bucket and inspect individual audit-object version retention.

Compliance mode prevents deletion or shortening of retention during the retention period even by root; governance mode permits bypass only with the necessary bypass authorization and request.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: On the prepared Object Lock bucket, apply the supplied default duration and mode. Inspect audit-object version retention and its retain-until date. For compliance mode, deletion or shortening is prevented during that period even by root. For governance mode, bypass requires the necessary bypass authorization and request. Record the mode and version-specific retention rather than describing all Object Lock retention as identical.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Governance and compliance modes have different bypass boundaries. Governance permits authorized requested bypass; compliance does not permit deletion or shortened retention during the period even by root. Check the individual audit-object version.

video_need.reason: A short version/mode/retain-until comparison helps distinguish governance bypass from compliance retention; text covers the rules.

practice_anchor.objective: Apply the supplied default retention duration and mode to one prepared Object Lock audit bucket, then inspect individual audit-object versions for their retention mode and retain-until date.
practice_anchor.success: The prepared bucket's default retention matches the supplied policy. Recorded version-specific modes and retain-until dates show whether the inspected audit-object versions remain protected for the supplied interval, with governance bypass distinguished from compliance protection. No unapproved retention settings are applied.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make each inspected audit-object version's retention mode and retain-until date visible alongside the supplied required retention interval, distinguishing governance's authorized requested bypass from compliance's prohibition on deletion or shortening during retention, even by root.

teaching_notes: Use prepared bucket and supplied retention policy; do not create irreversible unapproved compliance settings.

coverage.learning_objective: Configure and initialize an S3 Terraform backend

required_facts.statement: The S3 backend stores Terraform state in a specified bucket and key, separate from the configuration that declares managed resources.
Provision the protected backend bucket with the supplied local-state bootstrap configuration before selecting it as the backend.
Run terraform init -migrate-state after changing the backend, approve the supplied migration and verify state is at the intended bucket/key.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Terraform's remote state bucket must already exist before it can store state for the configuration that manages exercise resources. Keep backend bootstrap, backend selection and migration distinct.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The S3 backend stores Terraform state in a specified bucket and key, separate from the configuration that declares managed resources.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Provision the protected backend bucket with the supplied local-state bootstrap configuration. Substitute the actual supplied bucket, key and Region in the line-separated backend block. The block configures state storage; it is not the resource declaration that creates the bucket. After changing the backend, run terraform init -migrate-state, approve the supplied migration and verify state at the intended bucket/key. Keep the bootstrap result and migrated-state location with the record so the workflow does not assume a backend can create itself before initialization. Apply the supplied protection settings without introducing a new backend design or another storage service.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Backend configuration names an already-provisioned state location; it is separate from managed-resource declarations. Provision the backend bucket first, then initialize/migrate and verify the intended bucket/key rather than treating the HCL block as bucket creation.

video_need.reason: Local bootstrap, backend selection and state migration are distinct transitions best clarified in one HCL-to-state-location demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Use the supplied local-state bootstrap configuration to provision one protected S3 backend bucket. Configure the already-provisioned backend with the supplied bucket, key and Region, retain the supplied protection settings, then initialize and migrate the exercise state.
practice_anchor.success: The protected bucket exists before backend selection, the backend arguments match the supplied destination, and the approved migration places exercise state at the intended bucket/key.

live_code.required_skill: Configure an S3 backend using line-separated HCL arguments and migrate existing local exercise state to the supplied destination.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide a supplied local-state bootstrap configuration for one protected S3 bucket, the supplied BUCKET, KEY and REGION values, fixed protection settings, and a prepared means of inspecting the destination object. Leave backend selection until after bucket provisioning.
live_code.observable_success: Provisioning evidence shows the protected bucket existed before backend selection. The line-separated backend block uses the supplied values. Initialization completes after approval of the supplied migration, and destination inspection confirms exercise state at the intended bucket/key.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the sequence visible: supplied local-state bootstrap provisions the protected bucket; the backend block selects that existing bucket and key; approved initialization migrates state; destination inspection verifies the intended object location.

teaching_notes: Show line-separated HCL, not comma-separated shorthand; use supplied bootstrap and migrate-state approval.

required_facts.statement: By default Terraform destroys an object before creating its replacement; create_before_destroy requests the reverse order where supported.
prevent_destroy rejects a plan that would destroy the protected resource while that lifecycle rule remains in its configuration.

Set the supplied lifecycle argument in the resource block, introduce the controlled replacement-triggering change, and inspect the plan’s replacement order or prevention error before the approved permitted apply.
Lifecycle settings constrain replacement mechanics but do not replace scope and impact approval.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A replacement plan can have a permitted order or be prevented by a lifecycle rule. These controls affect mechanics, but the operator still needs scope and impact approval for a permitted change.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: By default Terraform destroys an object before creating its replacement; create_before_destroy requests the reverse order where supported.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
prevent_destroy rejects a plan that would destroy the protected resource while that lifecycle rule remains in its configuration.

Set the supplied lifecycle argument in the resource block, introduce the controlled replacement-triggering change, and inspect the plan’s replacement order or prevention error before the approved permitted apply.

Lifecycle settings constrain replacement mechanics but do not replace scope and impact approval.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Set the supplied lifecycle argument in the resource block and introduce the approved controlled replacement-triggering change. Inspect the plan's replacement order or prevention error. By default Terraform destroys the old object before creating its replacement; create_before_destroy requests the reverse where supported. prevent_destroy rejects a destruction plan while that rule remains in configuration. If the plan is permitted, follow the supplied approval before applying it. Record the order or rejection evidence separately from scope/impact authorization. Do not describe a lifecycle setting as a substitute for review or as a guarantee that every replacement can be performed with both objects coexisting.

Compare two approved controlled plans: one requests create-before-destroy where supported, while another destruction is rejected by a still-present prevent_destroy rule. The first record concerns ordering; the second concerns plan prevention. Neither result proves the change's business impact is acceptable. Scope review and approval remain necessary for the permitted plan, while the prevention error is evidence that the configured lifecycle boundary blocked that destruction.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: create_before_destroy is a request for reversed replacement order where supported, not a universal feasibility guarantee. prevent_destroy applies while its rule remains in configuration. Neither lifecycle setting replaces scope and impact approval.

video_need.reason: A planned replacement order or prevention error benefits from comparing controlled lifecycle configurations and their plan evidence.

After changing the configuration, the presenter attempts an automatically approved apply and receives an “instance cannot be destroyed” error. The presenter then explains that removing the lifecycle rule would permit the previously blocked change. This protection depends on the rule remaining in configuration; it does not establish that a permitted change is safe or authorized.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An isolated recovery target needs replacement EC2 infrastructure from a supplied CloudFormation template. Confirm authority, Region and parameters before creation, then verify recovery readiness beyond stack completion.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Creating a stack from a template provisions its declared resources under the target account’s execution authority and selected Region.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied restoration template, approved recovery credentials, explicit isolated target and required parameters to create the replacement EC2 stack.

Monitor stack events until creation completes, inspect resource IDs and outputs, and run the supplied instance and service recovery-ready checks.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case

Monitor stack events until creation completes. Inspect resource IDs and outputs, then run the supplied instance and service recovery-ready checks. teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence

context.concept_name: Block release on actionable dependency or image security findings

coverage.learning_objective: Gate release on actionable security findings

required_facts.statement: Inspector findings report vulnerability evidence, affected resources and severity that can inform release decisions.
Compare the supplied scan report with the stated severity threshold and documented exception policy to decide whether a finding is actionable.
Make the scan-policy check return failure for an actionable unexcepted finding and require its success before promotion; retain the report and policy decision as evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A release security scan is useful as a gate only when its evidence is compared with an explicit severity threshold and exception policy. The result should control promotion according to that policy.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Inspector findings report vulnerability evidence, affected resources and severity that can inform release decisions.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Compare the supplied scan report with the stated severity threshold and documented exception policy to decide whether a finding is actionable.

Make the scan-policy check return failure for an actionable unexcepted finding and require its success before promotion; retain the report and policy decision as evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Read the supplied Inspector report's affected resource, vulnerability evidence and severity. Compare findings with the stated threshold and documented exceptions. For an actionable unexcepted finding, make the supplied policy check return failure and require success before promotion. Retain the report and the policy decision. If a documented exception applies, record that policy basis rather than silently dropping the finding. This is a bounded release decision using supplied scan evidence, not a lesson in vulnerability exploitation, specialist remediation or inventing a new severity policy.

Compare an actionable unexcepted finding with one covered by a documented exception. Both remain scan evidence; the supplied policy determines their different gate outcomes. Retain the exception basis alongside the finding rather than claiming the scanner did not detect it. If a blocking policy result is tolerated by the workflow, the gate is not enforcing the stated precondition even though the scan ran.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A scan report alone is not an enforced release gate. The policy check must fail for actionable unexcepted findings and promotion must require its success. Also, severity should be read alongside the documented threshold and exception policy.

video_need.reason: A short scan-evidence/policy-outcome walkthrough helps apply the threshold and exceptions; no vulnerability exploitation demonstration is needed.

practice_anchor.objective: Using a supplied Inspector report, severity threshold, documented exceptions and pipeline controls, block one pipeline run on an actionable unexcepted dependency or image finding.
practice_anchor.success: The supplied scan-policy check returns failure for the actionable unexcepted finding, promotion remains blocked because it requires that check's success, and the report and policy decision are retained as evidence.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the supplied finding's vulnerability evidence, affected resource and severity alongside the threshold and exception decision, with the scan-policy check failed, promotion blocked and retained evidence accessible.

teaching_notes: Use supplied scan/threshold/exceptions; do not invent vulnerability facts or policy exceptions.

context.concept_name: Diagnose a failed delivery pipeline action

coverage.learning_objective: Diagnose a failed delivery pipeline action

required_facts.statement: Pipeline execution and action history identify failed actions and their error details.
Find the first failing action in the selected execution, inspect its input artifact revision and linked service logs, and use the error evidence to identify the correction.
Retest after the approved correction and verify that action succeeds before investigating later dependent actions that did not run.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A pipeline has stopped, and several later actions did not run. Start with the first failing action in the selected execution instead of treating every unrun dependent action as an independent failure.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Pipeline execution and action history identify failed actions and their error details.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Find the first failing action in the selected execution, inspect its input artifact revision and linked service logs, and use the error evidence to identify the correction.

Retest after the approved correction and verify that action succeeds before investigating later dependent actions that did not run.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Open the supplied execution and action history. Identify the first failing action, inspect its input artifact revision and follow its linked service logs. Use the error details to select the approved correction. Retest and verify that action succeeds before investigating later dependent actions that did not run. Keep execution and revision identities with the evidence so a successful retry of a different input is not mistaken for correcting this failure. The example follows the pipeline's dependency break and service evidence; it does not guess the cause from the name of a later blocked stage.

If the source action succeeded and the build action failed, start with the build input revision and build logs rather than diagnosing the deployment action that never ran. After the approved correction, verify the same required action can succeed with the intended input. That progression follows the execution's evidence and dependency structure, instead of turning every later unrun action into a separate root cause.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Not run is not the same evidence as failed with an error. Find the first failing action and its input/logs, retest the approved correction and verify success before investigating dependent actions that could not progress.

video_need.reason: Execution history, first failing action, input revision and linked service logs benefit from an evidence-led troubleshooting demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Diagnose one seeded CodePipeline action failure using supplied execution history, action error details, input artifact revision and linked service logs. Select the evidence-supported approved correction, then retest the action.
practice_anchor.success: Identify the first failing action in the selected execution, retain its execution and input revision identities, and select the approved correction supported by its error details and linked service logs. After the correction, verify that action succeeds with the intended input before investigating later dependent actions that did not run.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the selected CodePipeline execution with a successful source action, a failed build action and a deployment action that did not run. Make the failed action's input artifact revision, error details and linked service logs visible, followed by its successful retest with the intended input.

teaching_notes: Use supplied logs/error evidence; do not invent corrective commands or unsupported causes.

context.concept_name: Diagnose EC2 or container health failures using telemetry and prepared Linux inspection skills

coverage.learning_objective: Diagnose workload health failure from telemetry

required_facts.statement: EC2 system status checks concern underlying AWS host issues, while instance checks concern the instance’s software and networking.
Use the supplied metric and log time window to identify the affected workload, then inspect the component’s service status, events and logs rather than assuming the symptom proves its cause.
For a container, inspect container state, exit status and recent logs; apply the evidence-supported correction and repeat the supplied health check.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Telemetry shows a workload symptom, but the cause may be in the host, instance software or container. Combine the supplied time window with component inspection before changing anything.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: EC2 system status checks concern underlying AWS host issues, while instance checks concern the instance’s software and networking.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied metric and log time window to identify the affected workload, then inspect the component’s service status, events and logs rather than assuming the symptom proves its cause.

For a container, inspect container state, exit status and recent logs; apply the evidence-supported correction and repeat the supplied health check.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied metric/log interval to locate the affected workload. For EC2, read system status checks as underlying AWS-host evidence and instance checks as instance software/networking evidence. Inspect component service status, events and logs using the prepared Linux skills and supplied procedure. For a container, inspect its state, exit status and recent logs. Select the approved correction supported by that evidence and repeat the supplied health check. If a metric improved but the required health check still fails, retain that outcome rather than declaring recovery from a single signal. The symptom identifies what to investigate; it does not by itself prove the cause.

A component inspection result should be tied to the telemetry interval and affected resource. Logs from another component or time window may not explain this symptom. After the approved correction, compare the repeated supplied health check with the original failure. Keep any remaining failed checks visible; one improved metric or restarted process does not erase the application health criteria the task requires.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: System and instance status checks concern different boundaries. A metric or log symptom is not automatically its own cause. Inspect the component and repeat the supplied health check after an evidence-supported correction.

video_need.reason: Correlating workload telemetry with component state and repeated health checks benefits from a controlled diagnostic demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Resolve one seeded container health failure using supplied inspection tools: correlate the supplied metric and log time window with the affected workload, inspect component service status, events, container state, exit status and recent logs, and apply the approved correction supported by the evidence.
practice_anchor.success: The affected workload and failing component are correctly identified from evidence within the supplied time window. The learner applies the evidence-supported approved correction and repeats the supplied health check, confirming that the original failure is resolved rather than relying only on an improved metric or restarted process.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the supplied telemetry interval and affected workload alongside component inspection results, including container state, exit status and recent logs, with the original and repeated health-check results visible.

teaching_notes: Require external Linux service/process preparation; do not author new inspection commands or boot-startup configuration.

context.concept_name: Gate release completion on a deployed-service smoke check

coverage.learning_objective: Gate release completion on a smoke check

In the supplied Lambda validation action, call CodePipeline PutJobSuccessResult with the job ID only after a passing smoke check; call PutJobFailureResult on failure so dependent progression remains blocked.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Deployment completion must be followed by a live smoke check for the intended revision. The validation action should report success to CodePipeline only after the supplied behavior check passes.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A post-deployment validation action checks live application behavior rather than merely whether a deployment operation completed.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Run the supplied smoke-check action against the deployed endpoint and verify the expected response for the deployed revision.

In the supplied Lambda validation action, call CodePipeline PutJobSuccessResult with the job ID only after a passing smoke check; call PutJobFailureResult on failure so dependent progression remains blocked.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Run the supplied smoke-check action against the deployed endpoint and compare its response with the expected response for that revision. In the supplied Lambda validation action, send PutJobSuccessResult with the job ID only for a passing check. For failure, send PutJobFailureResult so dependent progression remains blocked. Keep the revision, endpoint result and reported job outcome in the evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A completed deployment operation is not a live application check. The smoke test validates behavior, and its passing result must precede PutJobSuccessResult. Report failure rather than advancing dependent progression when the supplied check fails.

video_need.reason: Live smoke response and success/failure reporting to the dependent pipeline benefit from a short validation-action demonstration.

segments.label: Why deployment success still needs a live-service smoke check
segments.summary: A successful deployment operation does not prove that the application works. Files can be copied and the application started, yet a configuration error or broken database connection can prevent useful behavior. Smoke checks test basic functionality immediately after deployment. Examples include reaching the home page with an HTTP 200 response, signing in with test credentials, and reaching a health endpoint. These checks are deliberately simple and fast—roughly one or two minutes—not comprehensive application testing.

bridge_note.before: Watch for the distinction between completing deployment operations and confirming live application behavior. The endpoint examples illustrate quick smoke checks, not comprehensive testing.
bridge_note.after: The clip explains why smoke checks matter, but omits supplied-action execution, deployed-revision verification, and Lambda job-result reporting. The text covers those steps, including blocking progression on failure.

practice_anchor.objective: Add the supplied Lambda smoke-check action after deployment in a prepared CodePipeline simulation. Configure its supplied deployed endpoint and expected revision response, then connect passing and failing check outcomes to the corresponding job-result reporting paths.
practice_anchor.success: The action checks the supplied endpoint against the expected response for the deployed revision. A passing check calls PutJobSuccessResult with the job ID; a failing check calls PutJobFailureResult and leaves dependent progression blocked.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show deployment completion followed by a supplied endpoint smoke check, with the expected deployed-revision response comparison branching to PutJobSuccessResult with the job ID on pass or PutJobFailureResult with dependent progression blocked on failure.

teaching_notes: Use supplied smoke action/Lambda scaffolding; do not teach application endpoint test authoring.

clusters.title: Recovery rehearsal readiness
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent checks prepare one bounded recovery rehearsal: verify the approved session's identity, lifetime and access, then verify the isolated restoration destination and client traffic. All recorded prerequisites precede the tile, with required external preparation still binding at entry. Session authorization and environmental isolation remain independent readiness checks; neither substitutes for the other and neither depends on learning its neighbor first.

clusters.title: Controlled and evidenced operational response
clusters.reasoning: Approval/stop controls and execution evidence are complementary parts of the same bounded response workflow. Their recorded prerequisites, including action authorization and CloudTrail attribution, are all available before this tile. Keep preventing or stopping an operation distinct from recording what actually executed: the audit record includes failed outcomes and cannot be inferred from approval or intended actions.
